title: The AI Fluency Imperative: Cognitive Tax, the Diamond Workforce, and the Case for Consequence-Based Learning
abstract: Generative and agentic AI are lowering the cost of producing knowledge work while leaving responsibility for its quality with people. This conceptual paper argues that the result is a cognitive tax, the effort of directing, verifying, and answering for synthetic output, and that the tax falls hardest where expertise is formed. Drawing on recent evidence on novice productivity, early-career employment, and managerial strain, it distinguishes three levels of capability: information literacy, AI literacy, and AI fluency. It defines fluency as a judgment-based capacity: setting boundaries for autonomous systems, calibrating human sign-off to consequence, auditing outputs adversarially, and deciding when AI should not be used. Because the entry-level roles in which such judgment was historically formed are contracting, the paper argues that AI fluency cannot be produced by adding AI content to existing courses. It proposes a two-stage developmental model: a foundation stage of deliberate cognitive friction in coursework, in which students attempt problems before consulting AI and are assessed on how they reconcile the two, followed by a consequence stage of clinical-model internships, client-based projects, and student venture teams. The paper closes with implications for assessment, curriculum, and partnerships, and with an agenda for research on measuring judgment.

title: AI Literacy
abstract: Children in contemporary school settings are daily consumers of AI-generated content — whether they know it or not. Recommendation feeds, synthetic images, AI-drafted text, and algorithmic advertising have become routine features of childhood digital experience, yet most K–12 curricula offer little preparation for navigating these environments critically. This chapter argues that schools bear a genuine responsibility to address this gap through deliberate, grade-appropriate AI literacy education oriented not merely toward using AI tools, but toward questioning and evaluating what those tools produce. Drawing on recent empirical work and theoretical scholarship across AI literacy, media education, and ethics, the chapter traces a developmentally staged curriculum pathway from early childhood awareness through secondary-level civic and ethical reasoning, while also highlighting key challenges in implementation such as teacher readiness, assessment alignment, and the limited geographic distribution of existing research.

title: A Sovereignty Centred Model of AI Literacy for African Higher Education
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence now mediates how knowledge circulates in higher education, and how it is validated once it does. Prevailing conceptions of AI literacy have not caught up: they remain anchored in competency inventories that treat epistemic context as a peripheral concern. This conceptual article argues that such framings misdiagnose the problem facing African universities. Where technological infrastructures are largely imported and externally governed, the development of technical proficiency in isolation does not produce learner autonomy; it can deepen the dependency it was meant to remedy. We advance the AI Literacy for Sovereign Learning (AIL-SL) model. Epistemic sovereignty, in this account, is no additional competency. It is what emerges when four capacities (cognitive-technical, critical-epistemic, ethical-normative, socio-cultural) develop in relation to one another. Six propositions state the conditions under which that emergence occurs, and the boundary conditions that limit each claim. Published reviews of AI literacy instruments lend the argument empirical support: sixteen scales now exist, and none has been validated across cultural settings. The field's measurement turn has outpaced its attention to context. We draw out implications for curriculum design and teacher preparation, and specify how each proposition might be tested.

title: K-12 AI literacy frameworks after generative AI: A scoping review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become a priority in K-12 education, yet frameworks for teaching and assessing it remain fragmented across grade levels, national contexts, and disciplinary traditions. This scoping review maps and synthesizes framework-level contributions to K-12 AI literacy published between January 2024 and December 2025. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, we searched four databases and grey literature sources, screened 204 unique records, and applied a purpose-built checklist covering five criteria: grade bands, competencies, critical constructs, assessment, and exemplars. Fifty studies met the inclusion threshold. The corpus spans 15 countries, with the United States (32%), Hong Kong (26%), and mainland China (12%) accounting for 70% of included studies. Frameworks defined AI literacy through cognitive, affective, behavioral, ethical, and social dimensions, but dimensional models used inconsistent labels and constructs, with limited crosswalk among them. The ABCE framework offered the closest approximation to a shared measurement tradition, with adaptation across three educational systems. Assessment and curriculum also developed largely in parallel: scale-development papers reported psychometric evidence without instructional sensitivity data, while curriculum papers assessed learning through lesson-linked tools that limited cross-study comparison. title: Exploring AI Literacy Through a Semester-Long Course
abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised questions about students' understanding of responsible use and academic integrity. This descriptive study examines students' experiences in a semester-long AI literacy course in a humanities program at a large public university in the United States. The course addressed AI history, capabilities and limitations, academic integrity, and ethical considerations, and provided structured opportunities to explore multiple tools. Pre-course (N = 31) and post-course (N = 25) surveys examined tool familiarity, reported use, perceived usefulness, awareness of limitations, and self-reported understanding of AI-related academic integrity. At the end of the course, respondents described more task-specific tool selection, greater attention to evaluating outputs, and increased confidence in identifying appropriate uses of AI. These findings reflect perceptions and reported practices rather than independently assessed AI literacy or ethical competence. Because the instruments differed, respondents were not individually matched, and no comparison group was included, the findings cannot establish causal improvement. The study discusses implications for AI literacy instruction in humanities and language education and for future assessment of students' AI-related knowledge and practices.

title: Understanding generative artificial intelligence literacy in higher education: Development and validation of an instrument
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering higher education, creating a need to assess students’ GenAI literacy (GenAIL). Drawing on existing GenAIL frameworks and related assessment instruments, this study developed and validated the Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale for College Students (GenAILS-CS) as an instrument for assessing GenAIL in higher education. Survey data from 658 undergraduates were split for exploratory (n = 329) and confirmatory (n = 329) factor analyses. Results supported a five-dimensional, 21-item structure covering cognitive understanding, skill application, critical reflection, ethical responsibility, and collaborative innovation. Evidence indicated acceptable-to-good fit, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, positive associations with GenAI use frequency, and measurement invariance across gender and grade level. The instrument could inform diagnostic assessment and targeted GenAIL support in higher education.

title: A Self-Study of Teacher Educators’ AI Literacy and Professional Development from a Digital Agency Perspective
abstract: After the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in 2022, research on AI literacy in education is a growing field. Less attention has been given to how teacher educators engage with these technologies in practice. Drawing on a digital agency perspective on professional knowledge and AI literacy, this study reports findings from an exploratory self-study. We investigate how we, as three teacher educators, engaged with GenAI in the design and delivery of Small Private Online Courses (SPOCs). Our study identifies four situated epistemic practices emerging through negotiated engagement with GenAI, which, to varying degrees, challenge our professional judgement and identity as teacher educators, taking practice-stabilizing and practice-transgressive forms. Each of these aligns with AI literacy dimensions described in existing frameworks. The findings show how AI literacy is enacted in situated contexts, where teacher educators’ professional judgement is central rather than a stable digital competence. The study contributes to research on teacher educators’ AI literacy and professional knowledge.

title: Academic librarians' perceptions of new skills, competencies and professional development needs in the AI age
abstract: Purpose This study examined academic librarians' perceptions of new skills and competencies, use of AI tools and professional development needs. Design/methodology/approach An online survey was distributed via professional networks, and data were collected and analysed from 155 valid respondents across Australia, European countries and the USA. Findings The findings demonstrate that the highly ranked new skills needed by academic librarians included AI tools and output evaluation, application of data governance and management, AI literacy instruction and integration of AI into curricula. The new competencies consisted of ethical implementation and governance, critical analysis and evaluation of AI tools and AI literacy and conceptual understanding of AI. AI tools could be used to improve information service provisions through responsible and ethical information management and discovery. Key training and knowledge areas included critical evaluation of AI-generated content. Hands-on tutorials with case studies and in-person or hybrid workshops were the most suitable training formats. Practical implications The findings are helpful and practical for academic librarians to develop new skills and competencies and support professional development and curriculum renewal. title: Intelligent workspaces: how AI tools are changing service models and workforce skills in academic libraries
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming service models, workflows, and workforce roles in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. It examines the extent to which AI adoption influences service delivery, professional responsibilities, staff competencies, organizational readiness, and the development of intelligent library workspaces. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative descriptive design based on twenty semi-structured interviews with librarians, information technology staff, and administrative personnel working in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. Participants were purposively selected based on their direct experience with AI-supported tools and technology-enabled library services. The interview data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's framework to identify patterns relating to AI-tool adoption, service transformation, workforce competencies, staff readiness, and implementation challenges. Findings The findings reveal four interrelated dimensions of AI-driven transformation in academic libraries. First, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent discovery systems, automated search applications, and plagiarism-detection tools are increasingly embedded in routine library operations. Second, AI is contributing to more automated, personalized, responsive, and digitally mediated service models. title: Co‐existing and co‐constructing with AI: Beliefs, practices, and professional readiness of online language coaches
abstract: Abstract This study examines how online Spanish language coaches, that is, trained native speakers who facilitate authentic conversational practice, perceive and use artificial intelligence (AI) in virtual language teaching. While previous research has predominantly focused on classroom teachers, we use a mixed‐methods design that includes a questionnaire and open‐ended responses from 96 coaches based in 15 Spanish‐speaking countries. We examine their familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its use, and views on how it may complement human interaction in language learning. Coaches see clear benefits in using AI for lesson planning, personalization, and idea generation, but they also express concerns about data privacy and ethics, misinformation, reduced critical thinking, and the loss of emotional connection and cultural authenticity. Regression analyses show that familiarity with AI and comfort using it are the strongest predictors of perceived usefulness and willingness to integrate this technology into practice. The findings suggest that professional development should strengthen AI literacy while preserving the interpersonal and intercultural dimensions of language learning. Clear institutional guidance is also needed on AI use and pedagogical approaches that integrate AI without diminishing meaningful human interaction.

title: AI Teacher-Preparation Interventions and Readiness in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Scoping Review for Tanzanian Primary Education
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly featured in education policy across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), yet evidence on teacher preparation, particularly for primary education, remains limited. This scoping review mapped interventions preparing teachers to use AI and synthesised evidence on teacher readiness in SSA, drawing implications for Tanzanian primary education. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, searches covered Scopus on 25 July 2026, ERIC on 10 October 2026, African journals, theses, grey literature, and reference lists. Of 375 records identified, 188 were screened, 83 reports were assessed, and 35 reports representing 33 studies were included. Six reports described interventions (Tier A), encompassing chatbot support, workshops, device-free AI activities, generative AI tools, and national teacher training. Rwanda’s national programme reached over 5,000 teachers but reported no evaluation. Only one intervention included a comparison condition, and none assessed changes in teaching practice. Tier B comprised 27 readiness or literacy studies across nine countries; six focused exclusively on primary or basic-school teachers, and seven involved teacher educators. Teachers generally expressed positive attitudes towards AI, but limited training, poor connectivity, inadequate device access, and high data costs constrained use. title: CHALLENGES AND ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS IN UTILIZING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR RESEARCH AMONG BUSINESS EDUCATION POSTGRADUATE STUDENTS
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in academic research, influencing the way postgraduate students in business education access, analyze, and interpret data. Hence, the study investigated the challenges and ethical considerations in utilizing AI-powered research tools among postgraduate students of business education in Kwara State. The study had two specific purposes: research questions and null hypotheses. Relevant literature was reviewed, and the research adopted a descriptive survey design. The primary instrument for data collection was a structured questionnaire titled Challenges and Ethical Considerations in Utilizing Artificial Intelligence for Research Among Business Education Postgraduate Students (CEUAIPSQ), consisting of 20 items. The instrument was pilot-tested at Ekiti State University, Ado-Ekiti. The questionnaire’s reliability was confirmed through Cronbach Alpha reliability test which yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.75. Demographic data were analyzed using frequency and percentages, while the research questions were analyzed using mean ratings and standard deviations. The null hypotheses were tested using independent samples t-test at 0.05 level of significance. The findings indicated that challenges such as the high cost of AI tools (=2.60; SD = 1.01), lack of institutional support (=2.62; SD = 0.60), and limited internet access (=2.52; SD = 0.95) hinder postgraduate students’ use of AI-powered research tools. abstract: هدفت الدراسة إلى الكشف عن واقع استخدام أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي لدى معلمي ومعلمات صعوبات التعلم في مدارس التعليم العام بمدينة جدة، من خلال تحديد مستوى معرفتهم بهذه الأدوات، ومجالات توظيفها في إعداد المحتوى والأنشطة، والقياس والتقويم، وإدارة البيانات، ودعم التعلم وتخصيصه، إلى جانب التعرف على اتجاهاتهم نحو استخدامها، ووعيهم بالأخلاقيات والمسؤولية الرقمية، واحتياجاتهم للتطوير المهني، وأبرز التحديات التي تواجههم. واعتمدت الدراسة المنهج المزجي وفق التصميم التفسيري التتابعي؛ إذ جُمعت البيانات الكمية باستخدام استبانة إلكترونية، ثم جُمعت البيانات النوعية من خلال مقابلات شبه منظمة لتفسير النتائج الكمية وتعميق فهمها. وتكونت العينة الكلية من (77) معلمًا ومعلمة، واقتصر تحليل مجالات الاستخدام الفعلي على (57) ممن سبق لهم استخدام أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي، كما أُجريت المقابلات مع (5) مشاركين. وأظهرت النتائج ارتفاع اتجاهات أفراد العينة نحو استخدام هذه الأدوات، وارتفاع وعيهم بأهمية توظيفها بصورة مسؤولة وآمنة، في مقابل تفاوت مستوى الاستخدام الفعلي بين مجالات الممارسة. وكشفت النتائج عن فجوة بين التقبل المهني المرتفع ومستوى التوظيف التطبيقي المتخصص، ولا سيما في القياس والتقويم، وإدارة البيانات، ودعم التعلم وتخصيصه. كما بينت المقابلات أن نقص التدريب التطبيقي، وضيق الوقت، والصعوبات التقنية، ومحدودية الدعم الفني تحد من انتقال المعلمين من الاستخدام العام إلى التوظيف التربوي المتخصص. وأوصت الدراسة بتطوير برامج تدريبية تطبيقية متخصصة، وإعداد أدلة إجرائية وأخلاقية، وتوفير الدعم الفني والتنظيمي اللازم لتوظيف هذه الأدوات بفاعلية وأمان في ممارسات صعوبات التعلم.

abstract: The mismatch between Generation Z's (Gen Z) high expectations of artificial intelligence (AI) and organisational AI practices has profound implications for vocational well-being in India's job market. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) using the lavaan package in R was used to test the path model. We triangulated our findings with 20 semi-structured interviews. title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

title: Democratizing AI Governance
abstract: Democratization of artificial intelligence governance has become an indispensable condition for keeping technological innovation in step with social values, legal standards, and human rights. This study delves into the inclusive participation, public deliberation, and civic education can enhance accountability and transparency in AI policy design. Such a shift beyond expert-dominated models to frameworks that meaningfully involve citizens and civil society, along with interdisciplinary institutions, is essential for effective governance. It underlines that the development of AI literacy is crucial so that individuals and their communities are in a position to meaningfully assess algorithmic decisions, detect bias, and demand compliance with ethical standards from technology providers. Similarly, institutional transparency and procedural justice are located as elements of public trust premised on openness regarding data use, algorithmic processes, and policy enforcement. title: AI Chatbots in the Voluntary Sector: A Sociotechnical Perspective on Access, Risk, and Governance
abstract: AI adoption in the voluntary and community sector is accelerating as organisations respond to rising demand, resource constraints, and pressure to widen access to services. Chatbots can support scalable, always-available service delivery for vulnerable groups. However, their use in frontline settings raises ethical and organisational challenges where care, trust, and accountability are central. We argue that chatbot deployment should be understood as a sociotechnical problem shaped by tensions between access and risk, automation and human judgement, personalisation and privacy, and user dignity. Drawing on an integrative review of AI governance, healthcare chatbot, and nonprofit literature, alongside illustrative examples from high-stakes service contexts, the chapter identifies the structural tensions shaping design, implementation, and oversight. It then proposes a dual-loop framework linking real-time service interactions with organisational monitoring, learning, and adaptation to help operationalise ethical principles in complex service environments.

title: Capacidad institucional para la adopción responsable de inteligencia artificial en el sector público ecuatoriano: Desafíos y oportunidades para la gestión pública
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector presents opportunities to transform administrative processes and services, but it demands institutional capacities that ensure responsible, transparent, and sustainable use. This study aimed to analyze the institutional readiness of the Ecuadorian public sector for the responsible adoption of AI. A qualitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and exploratory-descriptive study was conducted. Twenty key informants from various Ecuadorian public institutions were selected using purposive sampling. The results revealed uneven and evolving institutional readiness. While institutions possess basic digital infrastructure, receptive staff, and initial experience with AI tools, they exhibit limitations in interoperability, specialized training, planning, and systematization of AI adoption. The main gaps were concentrated in governance, the absence of specific protocols, data protection, transparency, human oversight, and the definition of responsibilities. The study concludes that the responsible adoption of AI requires the joint strengthening of technological, human, organizational, and regulatory capacities. The main challenge lies in bridging the gap between emerging technologies and the institutional maturity needed to integrate AI securely, traceably, and in a way that strengthens Ecuadorian public administration.

title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

title: Conformance as a Distribution: Delegation Contracts, Error Budgets, and the Allocation of Evaluation Authority in Use-Based AI Regulation
abstract: Use-based AI regulation assigns obligations by deployment risk but lacks an evidentiary object to carry them. A benchmark score is a property of a model; conformance of a deployment is a failure rate under a declared distribution of contexts, bounded by a scope and subject to expiry. We take the delegation contract of earlier work (frozen configuration, scoped claim, executable revision rule) and study it under strategic play between a deployer, an auditor, and an enforcement point. We ask whether a declared context mixture can be made truthful; whether an audit can be unbiased against a system that detects evaluation traffic; whether a certification error budget can sustain a long-lived deployment; whether an aggregate audit can support a per-subgroup guarantee; and whether an incident metric that counts system failures but not fallback costs ranks arrangements correctly. For each we give a mechanism and a proposition: a proper-scoring penalty on the declared mixture bounds the excess failure of a best-responding deployer by $O(λ^{-1/2})$ in the penalty weight; a commit-reveal audit drawn from live traffic is unbiased by construction and grades the evaluator with the same sample; a halving error budget drives certification coverage below $(1-p)^n$ while $α$-investing sustains it under a marginal false-certification guarantee; a per-subgroup guarantee costs audit size scaling as $1/m$ in subgroup mass; and any failure-only incident metric prefers withdrawal at every fallback

title: Generative AI in Managerial Decision-Making: A Systematic Literature Review of Trust, AI Literacy, and Decision Quality
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. title: Version‐Specific Performance of ChatGPT in Audiogram Interpretation: Comparison of ChatGPT‐4.0 and ChatGPT‐5.1
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical decision support, yet how successive versions of the same model compare on diagnostic tasks remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify version-specific changes in diagnostic performance by directly comparing ChatGPT-4.0 and ChatGPT-5.1 on standardized pure-tone audiogram interpretation. STUDY DESIGN: Comparative diagnostic performance study. SETTING: Controlled experimental study using audiograms generated with simulation software. METHODS: One hundred audiograms, including 20 with intentional masking errors, were generated using AudSim Flex® software and submitted to both model versions through a standardized 7-step diagnostic prompt based on ASHA criteria. Two board-certified otolaryngologists with audiological expertise independently scored each response on a 5-point Likert scale, yielding 1400 evaluations per model. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa, and model comparisons were performed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: Inter-rater reliability was acceptable overall (κ = 0.74-0.78), though agreement was lower for degree-of-loss classification with ChatGPT-5.1 (κ = 0.44). ChatGPT-5.1 scored significantly higher than ChatGPT-4.0 on 6 of 7 questions (P < .001), with effect sizes ranging from 0.53 to 0.94. title: Large language model-assisted modern programming pedagogy model: a perspective on teaching programming in the era of LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are a double-edged technology. They can serve as learning assistants in programming while simultaneously raising pedagogical and ethical concerns. Programming education researchers have responded by providing guidelines and recommendations on teaching, assessment, and the ethical use of LLMs. Although these developments are welcome, the literature still lacks theory-based frameworks that provide a philosophical grounding for programming pedagogy. This perspective paper addresses this gap by proposing the LLM-Assisted Modern Programming Pedagogy (LAMPP) model. The model aims to provide a theory-informed framework for systematically guiding the integration of LLMs into programming pedagogy. It proposes four design principles encompassing the core components of pedagogy (i.e., teaching, lesson design, engagement, and assessment). Ethics is included as an additional dimension because ethical concerns cut across all aspects of pedagogy. The LAMPP model proposes different mechanisms that may mitigate potential learning losses associated with inappropriate or excessive reliance on LLMs. Future studies should test the effectiveness of these mechanisms. The model may provide a basis for educators, researchers, and policymakers when considering policies, curriculum structures, course outcomes, assessment practices, and ethical guidelines related to programming pedagogy. title: Is Your Data Ready for AI? What Five Years of Reports from 26 Regulators Reveal About Data and AI Governance
abstract: Working paper reporting, in brief, a document study of the 129 College Performance Measurement Framework (CPMF) reports filed by the 26 health regulatory colleges of Ontario, Canada, for 2020–2024. Each report was scored on a nine-dimension data and AI governance rubric, and all 1,030 forward-looking commitments were traced across the five reporting cycles. In brief: regulators report completing 56% of what they commit to and about one commitment in five is carried over unfinished; data quality is the least-described dimension; no report describes an AI impact assessment or monitoring of AI in use; and once data capability is taken into account, organizational size explains much less of which commitments get stuck. title: CDIE: Risk Extension and Traceable Uncertainty in Organizational AI Risk Assessment
abstract: This methodological note introduces CDIE as a proposed framework for documenting confidentiality (C), availability (D), integrity (I), and risk extension (E) in organizational risk assessment involving artificial intelligence. Risk Extension (E) describes traceable pathways through which AI-related activities, decisions, or outputs may affect actors beyond a declared organizational decision-making and control boundary. Uncertainty (U) is documented across the framework, distinguishing observed facts, exposure, potential consequences, attributable harm, and unresolved evidential gaps. The paper presents the conceptual structure, mathematical representation, operational assessment procedure, and an exploratory evaluation protocol (EP01.2). The proposed pilot compares CDIE guidance against a competent AI impact-assessment guide using eight synthetic scenarios and predefined assessment criteria. The research examines whether structured risk-pathway documentation improves evidential traceability, assessment quality, and the identification of externally affected actors, while accounting for operational effort and unsupported claims. Research status: Methodological proposal, version 0.2. The empirical pilot has not yet been conducted. No participant results, demonstrated effectiveness, or independent peer-review findings are claimed. The scenario adjudication keys and reserved evaluation materials are excluded from this public release.

title: When Consent Cannot Bear the weight: Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic POWER and the Limits of Data Privacy Self-Management in Nigeria
abstract: Nigeria’s data protection laws rely on a borrowed foundation. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, like the regulation it replaced, treats the individual’s consent as the moral and legal centre of gravity of lawful processing, reiterating the control-based conception of privacy that Nigerian courts have read into section 37 of the Constitution. This article argues that artificial intelligence has undermined that foundation. Machine learning systems derive their value from processing that individuals cannot foresee, inspect, or meaningfully refuse: large-scale inference, profiling that outruns any disclosed purpose, the repurposing of ordinary data as training material, and the fusion of biometric identity infrastructures whose consequences cannot be withdrawn. Drawing on Nigeria’s own experience, including the compulsory linkage of the National Identity Number to mobile SIM cards, the opening of the national biometric database to security agencies, and the punitive analytics of digital lenders, the article shows that consent in the age of artificial intelligence functions less as a safeguard than as a ritual of authorisation that transfers risk to the very people it purports to protect. It contends that reform should shift the centre of gravity of Nigerian privacy law from individual control towards institutional accountability and data justice: enforceable purpose limitation, mandatory algorithmic impact assessment built on the Act’s existing machinery, genuine constraints

title: Artificial Intelligence and Constitutional Rights in India: Regulating Algorithmic Decision-Making, Bias and Accountability
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into policing, welfare administration, employment, credit, education, healthcare, judicial and legal systems, and public administration. Algorithmic systems may improve efficiency, consistency and the processing of large quantities of information, but they may also reproduce or amplify discriminatory patterns embedded in historical data and institutional practices. Where governmental decisions affecting individuals are informed or generated by algorithms, constitutional concerns arise regarding equality, non-discrimination, privacy, dignity, autonomy, freedom, procedural fairness and access to remedies. India does not presently possess a single comprehensive AI-specific constitutional accountability framework. Nevertheless, Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, together with administrative-law principles and the emerging data-protection and responsible-AI framework, provide a substantial foundation for regulating rights-affecting AI. This paper argues for a rights-based, risk-sensitive Indian framework incorporating algorithmic impact assessment, transparency, meaningful explanation, human oversight, independent auditing, institutional accountability and effective remedies.

title: The Fallacy of Algorithmic Infallibility: Socio-Legal Challenges to Economic Public Order and State Liability in the Era of Automated Governance
abstract: Abstract The progressive integration of artificial intelligence and automated decision-making (ADM) systems into the exercise of public administrative functions has generated a critical disruption in the structural foundations of administrative law. Contemporary states delegate decisions of profound socioeconomic impactincluding tax liability determinations, social security benefit allocations, and immigration controlsto algorithmic systems that operate as opaque constructs, inaccessible both to affected citizens and to the judiciary. This article argues that the uncritical adoption of these systems has entrenched what we conceptualize as the fallacy of algorithmic infallibility: a technocratic presumption that equates mathematical processing with neutral, error-free governance. Through a descriptive-analytical and comparative methodology, drawing on the doctrinal framework of administrative liability, the principle of motivated administrative acts, and international regulatory convergence (EU AI Act; OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible AI), this study examines four paradigmatic case studiesRobodebt (Australia), SyRI (Netherlands), BOSCO (Spain), and Pretoria/Siarelis (Colombia)to demonstrate that current liability regimes are structurally inadequate to address harms caused by state-deployed algorithms. The article identifies three central failures: the dissolution of the causal nexus in algorithmic harm attribution; the cosmetic nature of human-in-the-loop oversight

title: Critical Perspectives on Algorithmic Bias and Due Process in Criminal Adjudication
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence and algorithmic risk-assessment into criminal adjudication marks a shift from judicial discretion to data-driven governance. Proponents claim these tools eliminate bias and docket delays; however, this review demonstrates that algorithmic models instead institutionalize historical inequities under a veneer of scientific infallibility. By ingesting datasets corrupted by over-policing, machine-learning systems mistake enforcement patterns for objective behavioral forecasts, penalizing marginalized groups through proxy variables and feedback loops. Crucially, this automated turn conflicts with due process and equal protection. When private vendors assert trade-secret privileges to shield source code and feature weights, defendants are denied the right to confront adverse evidence and secure reasoned rulings. Furthermore, automation bias leads judges to defer uncritically to probabilistic classifications, delegating qualitative judicial authority to corporate actors. Synthesizing comparative frameworks across the United States, European Union, and India, this paper argues for constitutional supremacy. It proposes enforceable safeguards, including codified algorithmic discovery rights, mandatory human-in-the-loop limits, pre-deployment impact assessments, and strict exclusionary rules, to ensure technological modernization does not compromise human liberty.

title: Co-production in Community Empowerment through the Kampung Lali Gadget Social Innovation
abstract: Children’s increasing use of digital devices has encouraged community-based social innovations that provide alternative spaces for learning and play. This study examines the mechanism of co-production in community empowerment through Kampung Lali Gadget in Pagerngumbuk Village, Sidoarjo Regency. A qualitative case-study design was employed. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews and direct observation involving the founder/manager, activity facilitators, a neighborhood leader, residents, and parents, and were analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s interactive model. The findings show that co-production operates as a cycle linking joint planning, complementary role allocation, participatory decision-making, and learning-oriented evaluation. The village government provides policy support; managers and volunteers design and deliver activities; parents and residents contribute legitimacy, local resources, and feedback; while universities, media, nongovernmental organizations, and private actors extend program capacity and networks. However, opportunities to express ideas do not by themselves demonstrate an equal distribution of authority. Program sustainability depends on converting cross-actor contributions into organizational learning, volunteer regeneration, and adaptive programming. Co-production generates public value when participation is accompanied by role complementarity, meaningful influence over decisions, and repeated learning mechanisms.
